questions.q: Which edge deployment tier covers Raspberry Pi 4 / NVIDIA Jetson / Intel NUC devices with 4-16 GB RAM and intermittent WAN connectivity?
options: Tier 1: browser and mobile client
Tier 2: edge server / CDN PoP
Tier 3: on-premise gateway / industrial edge
Tier 4: near-edge / regional
questions.explain: Tier 3 is the on-premise gateway/industrial edge tier: Raspberry Pi 4, NVIDIA Jetson, or Intel NUC with 4-16 GB RAM, local NVMe, and intermittent WAN - the most capable edge tier, able to run a full vector database instance.

questions.q: Why is SQLite-vec presented as the most portable option for constrained edge devices?
options: It is a SQLite extension written in C adding a vec0 virtual table for flat KNN and quantized IVF search, shipped as a single shared library under 200 KB, running in-process with no network hop, daemon, or port
It requires a dedicated GPU to function
It only runs on SQL Server Express
It streams vectors from Pinecone on demand
questions.explain: SQLite-vec is a C extension under 200 KB implementing a vec0 virtual table (flat KNN + quantized IVF-style index). Because SQLite runs in-process there is no network hop, no daemon, and no port - ideal for mobile and browser-wasm deployments.

questions.q: In the chapter's Qdrant edge configuration, which settings keep the RAM footprint low on a constrained device?
options: enable_tls: true and telemetry_enabled: true

mmap_threshold_kb: 1024 (memory-map segments larger than 1 MB, reading from flash instead of RAM), always_ram: false for quantized vectors, telemetry_disabled: true, and a single max_optimization_thread
max_segment_size_kb set to the maximum possible value
Storing all vectors in RAM and disabling quantization
questions.explain: The edge config memory-maps segments over 1 MB (reads from flash, not RAM), lets quantized vectors be mmap'd too (always_ram: false), disables telemetry, limits WAL, and uses a single optimization thread - keeping a 500K-vector collection viable on a 4 GB device.

questions.q: According to the chapter, what does binary quantization do to the RAM footprint of 500K 1536-dimensional vectors in Qdrant?
options: Increases it from 3 GB to 6 GB for redundancy
Has no effect on RAM, only on disk
Reduces it to exactly 3.7 GB
Drops it from approximately 3 GB uncompressed to under 800 MB
questions.explain: A collection of 500K 1536-dimensional vectors uses approximately 3 GB uncompressed but drops to under 800 MB with binary quantization, making it viable on a device with 4 GB total RAM.

questions.q: What is the key difference between edge vector replicas and traditional relational read replicas, per the chapter?
options: Edge vector replicas accept writes while relational replicas do not
The vector index is an expensive artifact that takes time and compute to build - you cannot stream changes and reconstruct an HNSW graph incrementally the way you replay row changes into a B-tree
Vector replicas never need synchronization
Relational replicas cannot serve reads
questions.explain: The database analogy (central write master, edge read replicas) holds, but with one wrinkle: the vector index is an expensive artifact that cannot be rebuilt incrementally like a B-tree from WAL replay, making index synchronization the hardest operational problem in edge vector search.
